A.explanation: Far too small - $10^{-13}$ $\Omega \text{m}$ is about five orders smaller than any real metal at room temperature.

B.explanation: Correct - copper has $\rho \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-8}$ $\Omega \text{m}$, so the order of magnitude is $10^{-8}$ $\Omega \text{m}$.

C.explanation: Too large for a metal - $10^{-3}$ $\Omega \text{m}$ is more typical of a semiconductor or very poor conductor.

D.explanation: Far too large - $10^{2}$ $\Omega \text{m}$ is in the range of an insulator, not a good conductor like copper.

hints: Notice the question asks for resistivity $\rho$ in $\Omega \text{m}$, not resistance $R$ in $\Omega$ - it is a material property defined by $\rho = RA/L$.
Recall that copper is chosen for wires because it is an excellent conductor, so its resistivity must be extremely small, much less than $10^{-3}$ $\Omega \text{m}$.
Compare the powers of ten: metals are around $10^{-8}$ $\Omega \text{m}$, semiconductors are much higher, and insulators reach $10^{2}$ $\Omega \text{m}$ and above.
walkthrough: Identify what is asked: the order of magnitude of resistivity of copper, a very good metallic conductor, in $\Omega \text{m}$.
Recall the defining relation $\rho = RA/L$ and the learned value for copper, $\rho \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-8}$ $\Omega \text{m}$.
Take the order of magnitude: $1.7 \times 10^{-8}$ is closest to $10^{-8}$, not $10^{-13}$ or $10^{-3}$.
Check the other options: $10^{-3}$ $\Omega \text{m}$ would give far too much wire resistance, and $10^{2}$ $\Omega \text{m}$ would be insulating behaviour.
Therefore the typical order matches $10^{-8}$ $\Omega \text{m}$. This is option B
